sections.title: A capital drawn on an empty plain
sections.intro_md:
Most Indian cities grew. Chandigarh was drawn. In 1947 Partition took Punjab's capital, Lahore, and left millions of refugees looking for a new life. Four years later a famous European architect walked across a plain of mango groves and villages under the Shivalik hills and, within weeks, sketched a whole city on paper: numbered rectangles, roads ranked like blood vessels, a government quarter at the top like a head.

It was built. Today about 12 to 13 lakh people live in it, and it is a World Heritage city, a Union Territory claimed by two states, a magnet for cricketers and civil servants, and the place where a road inspector secretly built a kingdom out of rubbish. This day is about how a city made from nothing became one of the most argued-about places in India.

spotlights.name: Le Corbusier walks the empty site
spotlights.spot_it: A thin man in round black glasses and a bow tie, pointing across flat fields of mango groves and villages with the Shivalik hills behind.
spotlights.story_md: In February 1951 a 63-year-old Swiss-French architect who had never built a city stepped onto a plain at the foot of the Shivalik hills. There were 24 or so villages, mango groves, two seasonal streams and the temple of the goddess Chandi on a ridge nearby. Within weeks Le Corbusier and his team had redrawn an American plan into a grid of rectangular sectors, with a government quarter at the top against the hills. He would come back almost every year until 1964, staying in his cousin's house, while the city rose around buildings he had sketched in a Paris studio.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Chandigarh is one of very few cities on Earth drawn whole, on paper, by one architect, and then actually built.
spotlights.memory_hook: One architect, one blank plain, one pencil: a capital in a few weeks of drawing.

sections.title: The city in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
Chandigarh sits at the foot of the Shivalik hills, about 250 km north of Delhi, where Punjab and Haryana meet. It is small: **114 square km**. The 2011 census counted **10.55 lakh** people, almost all urban, at more than **9,000 per square km**. It was inaugurated on **7 October 1953** and has been a **Union Territory** since 1 November 1966, as well as the shared capital of Punjab and Haryana. The Governor of Punjab is also its Administrator.

It is rich and educated by Indian standards: per-capita income of about **₹4.3 lakh** (fourth highest in India), literacy of about 86% in 2011, and a Human Development Index among the top three. It also has one of India's lowest sex ratios, 818 women per 1,000 men. Hindi is spoken at home by about two-thirds, Punjabi by about a fifth, and English is the language of administration.

spotlights.name: The Tricity
spotlights.spot_it: From the air: a tight grid of green squares, with Mohali spilling west into Punjab and Panchkula north-east into Haryana, the border invisible on the ground.
spotlights.story_md: Chandigarh itself is only **114 square km**, smaller than many Indian airports' catchment towns. So it grew sideways into two other states. **Mohali** (officially Sahibzada Ajit Singh Nagar) is a Punjab city that shares Chandigarh's sector numbering, and **Panchkula** is a Haryana city planned in its image. Together the three hold well over 16 lakh people in the 2011 census and probably 25 lakh or more today. A resident can live in Haryana, work in the UT and watch cricket in Punjab on the same day. Even the airport is split: the runway is in Chandigarh, the terminal in Mohali.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The planned city stopped growing at its borders; the region did not, and now plans itself around it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three governments, one grid, one airport split down the middle.

sections.title: Hills, choes and a lake
sections.intro_md:
The city sits on a gently sloping plain of river gravel, about 300 to 370 m above sea level, between two seasonal streams that come down from the Shivaliks: the Sukhna Choe to the east and the Patiali Rao to the west. The slope was one reason the site was chosen: rainwater drains away on its own. The hills give the city its skyline and its silt; on a clear winter day after rain, the snow peaks of Himachal show behind them.

The climate is north Indian: hot summers over 40 °C, a monsoon from July to September, and foggy winters near freezing. Planned green belts, forests along the streams and the protected catchment behind Sukhna make it one of the greenest cities in India, with leopards, sambar and wintering ducks within the Union Territory.

spotlights.name: The Shivalik hills
spotlights.spot_it: A low, crumbly, scrub-covered ridge on the northern skyline, blue in winter haze, seen across Sukhna Lake from almost every open space in the city.
spotlights.story_md: The Shivaliks are the youngest and lowest wall of the Himalaya, built from gravel and sand washed off the rising mountains over the last 20 million years. They erode fast: every monsoon the streams, called **choes**, carry silt down into the plain. The same soft beds are one of the richest fossil grounds in Asia, full of ancient elephants, giraffes and apes. Le Corbusier made the hills the backdrop of the whole plan: the Capitol sits at the top so that the government buildings are seen against them, and the city's rule about building heights keeps the view open.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The hills gave the city its frame, its lake and its biggest headache: silt.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Himalaya's youngest foothills, the city's permanent backdrop.

spotlights.name: Sukhna Lake

where.label: Sector 1, at the foot of the Shivaliks

spotlights.spot_it: A long, shallow, man-made lake with a straight promenade on its dam, rowing boats and pedal boats, and the Shivaliks across the water.
spotlights.story_md: Sukhna was made in **1958** by damming a seasonal stream, the Sukhna Choe. It covers about **3 square km** and is shallow, about 2.4 m on average. Le Corbusier and the chief engineer banned motorboats and cars from the dam, so the 2 km promenade is still a place to walk, not drive. Silt is the enemy: the lake has lost roughly half its capacity, and citizens have turned out with shovels for voluntary desilting. Pierre Jeanneret's ashes were scattered here in 1970. On 15 October 2026 Sukhna became **India's 103rd Ramsar wetland**, Chandigarh's first.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The city's living room: where it walks at dawn, rows, sulks and celebrates.
spotlights.memory_hook: No motorboats, no cars, one architect's ashes, and since 2026 a wetland of world importance.

spotlights.name: Winter birds of Sukhna

where.label: Sukhna Lake and Sukhna Wildlife Sanctuary

spotlights.spot_it: Rafts of diving ducks with chestnut heads far out on the water, cormorants drying their wings on posts, and fish eagles over the reeds in winter.
spotlights.story_md: Each winter Sukhna becomes a stop on the **Central Asian Flyway**. Ducks and geese come down from Central Asia and Siberia to the shallow water and reed beds at the lake's eastern end. The Ramsar listing named the **common pochard**, a vulnerable diving duck, and the endangered **Pallas's fish eagle**; the endangered black pond turtle lives in the lake too. Behind it, about 26 square km of the Shivalik catchment were bought and planted with trees from the 1960s to hold back silt. That catchment is now the **Sukhna Wildlife Sanctuary**, with sambar, wild boar and leopards a few kilometres from a city of a million people.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A planned city's reservoir became, by accident, a wildlife refuge of international importance.
spotlights.memory_hook: Siberian ducks in a modernist lake, leopards in the hills behind it.

sections.title: Before the city
sections.intro_md:
The plain was never empty. Harappan farmers lived here about 4,000 years ago. Medieval and later rulers left small forts and temples: the fort town of Mani Majra, the old fort of Burail, and the shrines of Chandi and Mansa Devi in the foothills. Under the Sikh and then British rule this was Kharar tehsil of Ambala district, a land of wheat, sugarcane, mango groves and villages with names like Kansal, Kaimbwala and Attawa.

When the government chose the site in 1948, those villages were in the way. Most were bought out and flattened. A few, like Burail, survived inside the sectors and became the city's crowded, unplanned pockets. The new capital was named after the goddess whose hilltop shrine stood nearby.

spotlights.name: Harappan finds under Sector 17
spotlights.spot_it: Red clay pots, a few painted in black, displayed in a museum case with a label that places them under the modern city centre.
spotlights.story_md: Digging the foundations of the new city turned up a much older one. Pottery, a settlement and burials of the **Harappan** or Indus Valley culture, from around 2000 BCE, were found in the area of **Sector 17**, the planned 'heart' of the modern city. The finds, red ware jars and bowls typical of late Harappan villages in the Ghaggar basin, are shown in the city's museums. They place Chandigarh at the north-eastern edge of the Indus world, near sites like Ropar and Sanghol. The plain Le Corbusier was told to treat as a blank slate had been farmed and settled for 4,000 years.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The newest city in India sits on one of its oldest civilisations.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dig under the modern heart and you hit the Bronze Age.

spotlights.name: Chandi Mandir
spotlights.when: Old village shrine; city named after it in 1950s
spotlights.spot_it: A small whitewashed hilltop temple of the goddess Chandi, with saffron flags, now inside the grounds of the Army's Western Command.
spotlights.story_md: The city takes its name from this temple. **Chandigarh** means 'fort of Chandi', the fierce form of the goddess Durga, whose shrine stood on a rise near the chosen site. The temple is not in Chandigarh at all but in Panchkula district of Haryana, about 15 km from the city centre, beside the cantonment that houses the Indian Army's **Western Command**, itself called Chandimandir. Devotees crowd it at Navratri. A modernist city meant to be 'unfettered by the traditions of the past' was named after a village goddess by people who found her temple was the only landmark on the map.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most modern city in India carries the name of one of its oldest kinds of goddess.
spotlights.memory_hook: A goddess's fort on a modernist grid.

spotlights.name: The villages under the sectors
spotlights.spot_it: Look for crooked lanes inside the grid: Burail, Attawa, Buterla, Kajheri and Mani Majra are old villages the plan swallowed but never erased.
spotlights.story_md: Chandigarh was not built on empty land. The first construction phase affected **58 villages** and about 21,000 people by the account in the city's own planning history; their fields were bought under the Land Acquisition Act and many families were moved to resettlement colonies. A few villages were left standing inside sectors, and today they are among the densest, most unplanned parts of the city, full of rented rooms for students and workers. In Burail, now in Sector 45, the walls and gate of an old fort still stand among the houses. In 1966, 34 more villages came under the new Union Territory. The plan drew a clean city on paper; the people of the plain did not disappear.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The 'blank slate' of modern planning had people living on it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Under every tidy sector, a village that was there first.

sections.title: Why build a city from nothing
sections.intro_md:
In August 1947 the Radcliffe line cut Punjab in two. Lahore, its capital for centuries, went to Pakistan. East Punjab's government, high court and university became refugees themselves, working from Shimla and borrowed buildings, while millions of people crossed the new border in both directions.

Nehru decided that the answer was not to expand an old town but to build a new one: a capital and a symbol. The story of who would design it took three years and two continents. An American planner and a Polish architect drew it first, until a plane crash in Egypt ended that team. The Indian officials then travelled to Europe and came back with Le Corbusier, his cousin Pierre Jeanneret, and an English couple, Jane Drew and Maxwell Fry.

spotlights.name: A capital lost to Partition
spotlights.spot_it: Refugee trains packed inside and on the roofs, the image of the Punjab split in 1947.
spotlights.story_md: When the Radcliffe line was drawn in August 1947, Punjab's capital, **Lahore**, went to Pakistan. East Punjab was left without a capital, a high court, a university or a secretariat. Its government worked out of borrowed buildings in **Shimla**; its university and many families were refugees. Up to a million people died in the Punjab violence and about 10 million crossed the border. Several existing towns, including Amritsar, Jalandhar and Ambala, were considered and rejected. In 1948 the government chose a new site in Kharar tehsil, partly because it was central, had water and good drainage, and was far enough from the border.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Chandigarh exists because of a wound: it was built to replace a lost city for a displaced people.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lahore went west; the Punjab drew itself a new one.

spotlights.name: Nehru's brief
spotlights.spot_it: The line quoted on every plaque and in every guidebook: 'unfettered by the traditions of the past'.
spotlights.story_md: Jawaharlal Nehru wanted more than a capital for Punjab. He called for 'a new town, symbolic of the freedom of India, unfettered by the traditions of the past, an expression of the nation's faith in the future'. He backed the project in Parliament against critics who called it wasteful, visited the site repeatedly and stood by Le Corbusier when Punjab's politicians balked at the concrete. Later he admitted that he did not like everything the architect built, but said the city 'hits you on the head and makes you think'. Chandigarh was his manifesto in concrete, the companion of the dams he called the temples of modern India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the city was a political statement about independent India, not just a housing project.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city ordered to forget the past, named after a goddess.

spotlights.name: P. L. Varma
spotlights.spot_it: In the archive photographs: the Indian engineer in a suit standing between Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret.
spotlights.story_md: Parmeshwari Lal Varma was the Punjab government's chief engineer, and with the administrator **P. N. Thapar** he was the Indian end of the whole project. The two flew over the plains in 1948 to pick the site, went to the United States to hire planners, and in 1950 travelled to Europe to find a replacement after the planning team collapsed. Varma ran the Capital Project's engineers, argued with Le Corbusier about money and drainage, and is credited with Sukhna Lake. Guidebooks remember the European names; the city's water mains, roads and sewers are largely his.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without the Indian engineers and officials, the famous drawings would have stayed drawings.
spotlights.memory_hook: The man between the two cousins in the photo built the plumbing.

spotlights.name: Albert Mayer's plan
spotlights.spot_it: A fan-shaped master plan with curving roads and superblocks, tucked between two streams, that most visitors never hear about.
spotlights.story_md: The first planner of Chandigarh was an American. **Albert Mayer**, a New York planner who had met Nehru while serving in India as a US Army engineer in the Second World War, was hired in December 1949. His plan was a gently curving, fan-shaped city of 'superblocks', self-contained neighbourhoods with their own schools and shops, cut by roads that kept fast traffic away from houses. Le Corbusier later straightened the curves into a grid, but kept the neighbourhood idea, the head-of-the-city Capitol and the green belts. Mayer received little credit for it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The sector, Chandigarh's basic unit, began as an American garden-city idea.
spotlights.memory_hook: An American drew the bones; a Swiss-French architect took the credit.

spotlights.name: Matthew Nowicki
spotlights.spot_it: A Polish architect known for the swooping saddle roof of the Dorton Arena in North Carolina, who was to design Chandigarh's buildings.
spotlights.story_md: Mayer's partner for the buildings was the brilliant Polish architect **Maciej (Matthew) Nowicki**, then teaching in the United States. He spent weeks in India in 1950 sketching a Capitol, houses and a market, drawings that still circulate among architects. On his way home in August 1950 his plane crashed in the Egyptian desert and he was killed, aged 40. Mayer did not want to go on without him, and the Punjab officials went to Europe looking for a new team. That search ended at Le Corbusier's studio in Paris. One air crash changed the look of a whole city.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Chandigarh looks like Le Corbusier because of an accident.
spotlights.memory_hook: A plane went down in Egypt, and a city in Punjab changed shape.

sections.title: Reading the plan
sections.intro_md:
Chandigarh's plan is simple enough to learn in ten minutes, and once you know it you can find anything. The city is a grid of rectangular **sectors**, numbered in a zigzag from Sector 1 at the top (the Capitol) downwards. Fast roads run between sectors; each sector looks inward to its own market and green strip. A park, the Leisure Valley, runs through the city like a spine.

Le Corbusier explained it as a body and ranked its roads in seven types. He also tried to protect it from the future, with a law banning building in a belt around the city and an edict of rules carved in stone. Much has been bent since: the population is more than twice what the first phase was built for, and the tricity has spread far beyond the grid.

spotlights.name: The sector
spotlights.spot_it: A rectangle about 800 m by 1,200 m, walled by fast roads with no gates opening on them, with a green strip and a shopping street running through the middle.
spotlights.story_md: The sector is the cell of the city. Each is about **800 by 1,200 m**, sized so that a family can walk to its school, clinic, market and park in about ten minutes. The fast roads around it (V3s) have no house doors opening onto them; you enter through a few gaps. Inside, a bazaar street (V4) cuts across one way and a green belt runs the other. There are 30 sectors in the first phase and 17 in the second. Addresses are written as house number and sector, so 'House 57, Sector 5' is all a letter needs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned an abstract planning idea into a daily rhythm: everything in your sector, the rest of the city by car.
spotlights.memory_hook: A village of 10,000 people in a 800 by 1,200 m box.

spotlights.name: The Seven V's
spotlights.spot_it: Wide, tree-lined fast roads with no frontage between sectors, then smaller and slower roads inside, down to footpaths through the green belts.
spotlights.story_md: Le Corbusier sorted traffic like blood vessels into **seven types of road**, les Sept Voies. V1 roads link the city to other cities. V2 are the great avenues such as Madhya Marg and Jan Marg. V3 are the fast roads between sectors. V4 is the shopping street through each sector, V5 the loop inside it, V6 the lane to the house, and V7 the paths through the green belts (a V8 for cycles was added later). The system is why Chandigarh has fast roads with no shopfronts and why it is pleasant to drive. It is also why it has more vehicles than people.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The road hierarchy shaped everything from traffic to how lonely a main road feels at night.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven road types, from city highway to garden footpath.

spotlights.name: The missing Sector 13
spotlights.spot_it: Count the sector signs: 12, then 14. There is no Sector 13 in the original plan.
spotlights.story_md: Sector numbers in the first plan run from 1 at the Capitol to 47, but **13** is missing. The usual explanation is the Western superstition about the number, and planners have never seriously disputed it. Sector 14 holds Panjab University; Sector 12 holds PGIMER and the engineering college. Decades later the name was finally used for a new area on the eastern edge near Mani Majra, so today there is a Sector 13 of sorts, though old Chandigarh residents still say it does not exist.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rational, modernist plan quietly obeyed a superstition.
spotlights.memory_hook: The most logical city in India still skips 13.

spotlights.name: Sector 17 plaza
spotlights.spot_it: A vast paved square of grey concrete blocks with arcades on all sides, fountains, pigeons, the Neelam cinema and young people loitering in the evening.
spotlights.story_md: Sector 17 is the 'heart' of the plan, a car-free shopping and office centre built around a huge pedestrian plaza. Its four-storey blocks, designed by Le Corbusier's team, have deep verandahs that give shade in summer and shelter in monsoon. The Neelam cinema, the old bus stand and the state library sit around it. For decades this was where Chandigarh went to shop, flirt and be seen; it is still the venue for New Year's Eve and concerts. Malls in the suburbs have taken much of its business, and the city keeps trying to bring it back.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The city's one great public square shows how modernists imagined Indian street life.
spotlights.memory_hook: The heart of the body: a plaza you can cross without meeting a car.

sections.title: The Capitol Complex
sections.intro_md:
At the top of the city, against the hills, Le Corbusier placed his masterpiece: a vast concrete plaza with three great buildings, the **High Court**, the **Palace of Assembly** and the **Secretariat**, and a set of monuments. A fourth building, the Governor's Palace, was never built. In July 2016 the complex was inscribed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, one of 17 works by Le Corbusier across seven countries.

The Capitol is a lesson in building for heat: roofs that float like umbrellas, walls of sunshades, pools that cool the air and reflect the buildings. It is also a lesson in how monuments age. Security fences cut the plaza, pools have dried, and the government that uses it is split between two states. Guided tours run from the tourist office; photography inside is restricted.

rows.High Court: Three pylons in green, yellow and red
rows.Palace of Assembly: Enamel door painted by Le Corbusier

spotlights.name: Punjab and Haryana High Court
spotlights.spot_it: A long concrete umbrella roof floating on arches, and three giant pylons at the entrance painted green, yellow and red.
spotlights.story_md: The first building of the Capitol, opened in **1955**, the High Court is a box of courtrooms under a separate **parasol roof**, a vaulted concrete umbrella that shades the building and lets wind blow through the gap. The entrance is a ramped hall of three soaring piers painted in primary colours. Le Corbusier designed giant wool **tapestries** for the courtrooms, woven in Kashmir, partly to soak up the echo of concrete. It is the first building in the city made entirely of reinforced concrete, and it still serves two states: the Punjab and Haryana High Court, set up in 1947 in Shimla.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Its umbrella roof is a lesson in designing for a hot climate without air conditioning.
spotlights.memory_hook: A courthouse under a concrete umbrella, guarded by three painted giants.

spotlights.name: Palace of Assembly
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy concrete block with an upturned, gutter-like portico, reflected in a pool, with a tilted pyramid and a flared tower poking out of its roof.
spotlights.story_md: The **Palace of Assembly** houses both the Punjab and the Haryana legislatures. From outside you see a great curving portico, like a gutter turned to the sky, standing on thin fins. On the roof sits the top of the assembly chamber: a **hyperbolic tower**, its shape borrowed from the cooling towers of power stations, open to the sky to let in light. A tilted pyramid over the upper house is lined up with the sun for a ceremony Le Corbusier imagined but nobody holds. The building took 11 years and was inaugurated in April 1964.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Two state governments meet under one modernist roof, a constant reminder of the city's split ownership.
spotlights.memory_hook: A parliament crowned by a cooling tower.

spotlights.name: The enamel door
spotlights.spot_it: A huge pivoting ceremonial door covered in bright enamel panels: a sun, a tree, a bull, a turtle and the path of the sun across the sky.
spotlights.story_md: The ceremonial entrance of the Assembly is a single enormous **pivoting door**, covered in enamelled steel panels painted by Le Corbusier. Nehru asked him to make imagery for the new nation; he answered with his private cosmology: the sun's daily and yearly paths, a serpent, a tree, a bull, a tortoise, a human figure and his own symbols of water and earth. The panels were made in France and, the story goes, flown to India. The door is opened only on rare state occasions, so most people see it closed, which is when you can read it best.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most complete painting Le Corbusier made for any building.
spotlights.memory_hook: A door that is a sky map, opened almost never.

spotlights.name: The Secretariat
spotlights.spot_it: A 254 m long slab of concrete, eight storeys high, its face a honeycomb of sunshades, with a sculptural ramp tower at the front.
spotlights.story_md: The **Secretariat** holds the offices of both state governments in one slab about **254 m long and 42 m tall**, made of six blocks joined at expansion joints. Its face is a deep grid of concrete sunshades, the **brise-soleil**, that Le Corbusier developed for hot climates; behind them, each office got light without glare. Ministers' offices are marked by a different rhythm in the middle. Two great ramps let clerks climb on foot, and there is a roof garden from which the whole Capitol can be seen. Visitors rarely get inside because of security.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the largest building Le Corbusier ever completed.
spotlights.memory_hook: A quarter-kilometre of sunshades.

spotlights.name: The Open Hand
spotlights.spot_it: A giant metal hand, palm open and fingers up, on a mast above a sunken pit, which turns like a weathervane in the wind.
spotlights.story_md: The **Open Hand** is Chandigarh's emblem: 'open to give, open to receive'. Le Corbusier dreamed of it from 1948 and sketched the final design in 1964 for Nehru's 75th birthday. Both men died before it was built. It was finally put up in **1985**, 20 years after the architect's death, using his drawings. The sheet-metal hand is **14 m high and weighs about 50 tonnes**, on a 26 m structure. It sits on ball bearings, so it **turns with the wind** like a vane. Below it is a sunken amphitheatre, the 'Trench of Consideration', meant for public debate.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the city's logo, on its seal, its signs and its police uniforms.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 50-tonne hand that turns to face the wind.

spotlights.name: Tower of Shadows
spotlights.spot_it: An open concrete cube of sunshades with no walls or windows, oriented exactly to the compass points.
spotlights.story_md: The **Tower of Shadows** has no use except to teach. It is an open frame of louvres aligned to north, south, east and west, built to demonstrate that well-designed sunshades can keep the sun off a space at every hour and season while letting the breeze through. Le Corbusier worked out the angles from sun-path diagrams, the same method he used for the Secretariat and the High Court. On a hot afternoon you can walk in and feel the difference. It sits on the Capitol's huge open plaza between the Assembly and the High Court.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A building made only to prove an idea about climate.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four walls of shade and no walls at all.

sections.title: The people who drew it
sections.intro_md:
Chandigarh is sold as Le Corbusier's city, but he spent only a month or so in India each year. The master plan and the Capitol were his. Most of what people live in, the houses, schools, shops, colleges and furniture, was designed by a team on the ground: his cousin **Pierre Jeanneret**, who stayed 14 years; the English couple **Jane Drew** and **Maxwell Fry**; and a group of young **Indian architects and engineers**, including one of India's first women architects.

The Indian side is often forgotten. Officials such as P. N. Thapar and P. L. Varma chose the site, hired the planners and fought for the budget. Indian architects drew the details and later ran the city's architecture department, spreading the 'Chandigarh style' across Punjab and Haryana.

spotlights.name: Le Corbusier
spotlights.spot_it: Round thick black glasses, a bow tie, a pipe and a sketchbook: the most famous architect of the 20th century.
spotlights.story_md: Born Charles-Édouard Jeanneret in Switzerland in 1887, he renamed himself **Le Corbusier** and became the loudest voice of modern architecture: houses as 'machines for living in', cities of towers and highways. Most of his grand city plans, including one to flatten central Paris, stayed on paper. Chandigarh was his only chance to build a city, though he designed only the master plan and the Capitol and a few buildings. He worked on it from 1951 until his death by drowning in the Mediterranean in **1965**. His Capitol is now part of a World Heritage listing of 17 of his works across seven countries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Chandigarh is the one place where his urban dream was tested in real life.
spotlights.memory_hook: The architect who wanted to rebuild Paris got Punjab instead.

spotlights.name: Pierre Jeanneret
spotlights.spot_it: A quiet man in his cousin's shadow, seen on a scooter or a bicycle on site; his house in Sector 5 is now a museum.
spotlights.story_md: Le Corbusier visited; his cousin **Pierre Jeanneret** stayed. He lived in Chandigarh from 1951 to 1965, as chief architect of the city and later adviser to Punjab, designing houses, schools, much of **Panjab University**, the Gandhi Bhawan and thousands of pieces of furniture. He trained a generation of young Indian architects and is said to have loved the city more than Paris. He died in Geneva in 1967; by his own wish his ashes were brought back and scattered in **Sukhna Lake**. His house in Sector 5 opened as a museum in 2017.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He did most of the everyday building that makes Chandigarh a city, not just a Capitol.
spotlights.memory_hook: The cousin who stayed, and whose ashes are in the lake.

spotlights.name: Jane Drew and Maxwell Fry
spotlights.spot_it: A married English couple of modern architects, fresh from building schools and housing in West Africa, in the first team photos.
spotlights.story_md: Jane Drew and Maxwell Fry were the English half of the original team. Nehru asked them after seeing their tropical work in West Africa, and it was Drew who persuaded Le Corbusier to take the job. In three years they designed much of the early **housing**, as well as schools, clinics and shops, using local brick and deep verandahs. Drew tested prototype houses with the families who were to live in them and asked them for criticism. Rents for the cheapest houses were capped at a tenth of a tenant's income. Their contract ran out in 1954, and they went home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Their humane, low-cost housing gave the city its liveable texture.
spotlights.memory_hook: The couple who got Corbusier on the plane, then built the houses.

spotlights.name: Urmila Eulie Chowdhury
spotlights.spot_it: A woman architect in a sari among the men of the Chandigarh team; later chief architect of two states.
spotlights.story_md: Urmila Eulie Chowdhury, born in 1923, studied architecture at the University of Sydney and joined Le Corbusier's team in 1951, one of the first women architects in India. She designed the Government Home Science College, the Women's Polytechnic and ministers' houses, adapted Jeanneret's furniture, and is credited with him for a version of the **Chandigarh chair**. She translated Le Corbusier's *Three Human Establishments* into English. Later she became **Chief Architect of Haryana** (1970) and **of Punjab** (1976 to 1981). She died in Chandigarh in 1995, mostly forgotten until recent scholarship rediscovered her.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The city's founding story usually forgets its Indian architects, and she was one of the best.
spotlights.memory_hook: The woman in the team photo who ended up running two states' architecture.

spotlights.name: The Indian team
spotlights.spot_it: Names on drawings, not plaques: M. N. Sharma, Aditya Prakash, B. P. Mathur, Shivdatt Sharma, J. S. Dethe, Jeet Malhotra and others.
spotlights.story_md: Behind the European names stood young Indian architects and engineers who drew most of the city. **M. N. Sharma** became Chandigarh's first Indian chief architect. **Aditya Prakash** designed the **Tagore Theatre** (1961) and spent his life arguing for self-sufficient, low-waste cities. **Shivdatt Sharma** worked with M. N. Sharma and Le Corbusier on the Government Museum, and **B. P. Mathur** on the university campus. Many went on to design across north India, spreading a 'Chandigarh style' of exposed brick, concrete frames and sunshades to Punjab and Haryana towns.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The modernist look of north India's towns spread from this drawing office.
spotlights.memory_hook: The team photo's back row built north India.

sections.title: Chairs, drains and a stolen heritage
sections.intro_md:
To furnish a city from scratch, Pierre Jeanneret's team designed everything: chairs, desks, beds, library racks, lamps, even manhole covers. They were made by local carpenters and foundries from teak, cane and cast iron, and were meant to be cheap and tough.

For decades nobody valued them. Then, from the late 1990s, European and American dealers discovered them. Truckloads of 'junk' bought at government auctions, and later pieces carried out of offices, ended up in galleries in Paris, New York and Seoul. A 2011 ban did not stop the trade. In June 2026, for the first time, the city got a foreign auction stopped. It is the most vivid story of what Chandigarh is worth to the world, and what it nearly lost.

data.label: Sales abroad since 2009
data.note: one count by a city activist

spotlights.name: The master-plan manhole cover
spotlights.spot_it: A cast-iron drain cover in the pavement whose raised pattern is the city's own master plan: the grid of sectors, the Capitol at the top and the lake.
spotlights.story_md: Le Corbusier's team put the plan of the city on its drains. Chandigarh's cast-iron **manhole covers** carry a relief map of the master plan, the rectangles of the sectors, the main roads and the Capitol, so that residents literally walk on the plan every day. Like the furniture, they are reported to have become collectors' items, dug up and sold. One even turned up as far away as a hospital in Shimla, a reminder of how the old Punjab capital's works department moved its stock around.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the city's design ambition reduced to its smallest, most everyday object.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city that prints its own map on its drains.

spotlights.name: The Chandigarh office chair
spotlights.spot_it: A teak frame shaped like an upside-down V on each side, with a woven cane seat and back: the chair in every government office and every design magazine.
spotlights.story_md: Pierre Jeanneret and his team designed thousands of pieces for the city's offices, courts, hostels and colleges: desks, library tables, file racks and above all **chairs**. They were made by local carpenters in **teak and cane**, with no fancy joints, cheap to build and easy to repair. For decades they sat in dusty offices and were sold off as junk in government auctions for a few hundred rupees. Today a single armchair can sell abroad for tens of lakhs of rupees, and copies are sold worldwide as the 'Chandigarh chair'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A government office chair became one of the most copied design objects of the century.
spotlights.memory_hook: From scrap auction to design icon, in teak and cane.

spotlights.name: Chandigarh's furniture goes abroad
spotlights.spot_it: An auction catalogue page in Paris or New York showing a battered cane chair with a Chandigarh building's paint mark on its leg.
spotlights.story_md: From the late 1990s, foreign dealers began buying Jeanneret furniture from government scrap auctions and, later, from people who simply carried it out of offices. In February 2011 the Home Ministry banned the sale and export of Chandigarh's heritage furniture. The trade went on: one count finds **more than 100 sales abroad since 2009, worth an estimated ₹40 to 50 crore**. In **June 2026**, for the first time, an overseas sale was stopped: two chairs said to have been stolen from Panjab University and PGIMER were pulled from a Paris auction after the Chandigarh administration filed two FIRs and the Centre intervened with France.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a case study in how heritage is lost: not by bombs, but by neglect and the market.
spotlights.memory_hook: A chair stolen from a university office, stopped at a Paris sale in 2026.

sections.title: A museum, a university and a hospital
sections.intro_md:
Beyond the Capitol, the buildings that matter most to people are the ones that came from Partition. The **Government Museum** in Sector 10 holds India's share of the Lahore Museum. **Panjab University**, founded in Lahore in 1882, was reborn as a refugee institution and now fills Sectors 14 and 25. **PGIMER**, the giant hospital in Sector 12, serves five states.

Architecturally, the campus and museum show how the city's designers worked: exposed brick, raw concrete, deep shade, water and greenery. The best single building outside the Capitol is probably Jeanneret's Gandhi Bhawan, a concrete flower in a pool.

spotlights.name: Government Museum and Art Gallery
spotlights.spot_it: A low, closed brick box raised on concrete stilts with a flat roof and a ramp, set on a lawn in Sector 10.
spotlights.story_md: Le Corbusier's museum in Sector 10, finished after his death and opened in **1968**, was designed as a growing museum that could be extended. Its collection began with Partition. On 10 April 1948 the treasures of the **Lahore Museum** were divided: about 60% stayed in Pakistan and 40% came to India. The Indian share became the core here, including **627 Gandhara sculptures**, the second-largest collection in India. Add one of the best collections of Pahari miniature paintings, and a natural history wing with Shivalik fossils, and it is the most underrated museum in north India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Its galleries hold half of what Punjab's lost capital once displayed.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lahore's treasures, split 60:40, and India's 40 live here.

compare.difference: Lahore kept about 60% of the shared collection, including the famous Fasting Buddha; Chandigarh got about 40% and built a modernist home for it.

spotlights.name: Gandhara Buddhas and Kangra paintings
spotlights.spot_it: Grey schist Buddhas with wavy hair and robes falling in Greek folds; and small, jewel-coloured paintings of Krishna and lovers in Himalayan landscapes.
spotlights.story_md: The museum's two great collections show two very different worlds. The **Gandhara** sculptures, carved in grey schist in what is now north-west Pakistan in the first centuries CE, show the Buddha in human form with the curls and draped robes of Greek and Roman art: the meeting of India and the Mediterranean in stone. The **Pahari paintings**, mostly from the Kangra school of the late 18th and early 19th centuries, show lovers waiting in storms, Krishna in the forest and nayikas of every mood, in fine lines and clear colour. Both came from places that are now outside Punjab.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Two of the finest art traditions of the subcontinent sit a short walk from Sector 17.
spotlights.memory_hook: Greek-looking Buddhas and Himalayan lovers, under one modernist roof.

spotlights.name: Gandhi Bhawan
spotlights.spot_it: A concrete building that rises from a square pool in three sweeping petals, as if a lotus or a bird were opening on water.
spotlights.story_md: Pierre Jeanneret's most loved building is a small study centre for Gandhian thought at Panjab University. Its roof rises in three curved concrete wings from a reflecting pool, so the building seems to float. Some see a lotus, some a bird, some hands in prayer. Inside is a library and a hall for lectures on non-violence. It was built in 1962 at the centre of the university's campus, which Jeanneret designed in exposed brick and concrete from the late 1950s. At night, lit up and reflected in the water, it is the city's most photographed modern building after the Capitol.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proves Jeanneret was a designer of poetry, not just of sensible housing.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lotus of concrete floating in a pool.

spotlights.name: Panjab University
spotlights.when: Founded Lahore 1882, campus in Chandigarh from 1956
spotlights.spot_it: A long campus of red brick and grey concrete: a library with tall fins, a student centre with a ramp, and a giant Le Corbusier-style administrative block.
spotlights.story_md: Panjab University was founded in **Lahore in 1882**. Partition split it too: the old campus became the University of the Punjab in Pakistan, and the Indian half became a refugee university, run from camps and borrowed rooms in Solan, Shimla, Jalandhar and Delhi. In 1954 it bought over 300 acres in Sector 14 and moved in from 1956. Jeanneret and his team designed most of its buildings. Its students and teachers include Prime Minister **Manmohan Singh**, who studied and later taught economics there, and generations of the officers, doctors and judges of Punjab and Haryana.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A university of refugees became one of north India's biggest.
spotlights.memory_hook: Born in Lahore, exiled to camps, reborn in Sector 14.

sections.title: Nek Chand's secret kingdom
sections.intro_md:
While the planners built the most orderly city in India, one of their employees was quietly breaking all its rules. **Nek Chand**, a refugee who became a road inspector, spent his evenings and weekends from about 1957 turning the city's waste into thousands of figures in a hidden patch of forest near the Capitol. Nobody gave him permission. When officials found it in 1975, it was already 12 acres.

The city chose to keep it. The **Rock Garden** opened in 1976 and is now Chandigarh's most visited place, a maze of passages, courtyards, waterfalls and armies of figures dressed in broken crockery. It is the opposite of the Capitol: small, handmade, playful and personal. Many visitors find it the more moving of the two.

data.label: Sculptures
data.note: plus a museum of 200 rag dolls

spotlights.name: Nek Chand Saini
spotlights.spot_it: A small, smiling man in a white kurta and a cap, standing among an army of figures made of broken bangles and tiles.
spotlights.story_md: Nek Chand was born in 1924 in Barian Kalan, near Shakargarh, in what is now Pakistan, and came to India as a Partition refugee. In **1951** he became a **road inspector** in Chandigarh's public works department. While the city was being built, he cycled around picking up waste: broken crockery, bangles, tiles, electrical fittings, rocks from the river beds, debris from the villages being demolished. From about **1957** he began secretly building a kingdom of figures in a patch of forest. He had no permission. He received the Padma Shri in 1984 and died in 2015, aged 90.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is India's most famous outsider artist, and he worked as a government clerk.
spotlights.memory_hook: A road inspector who built a kingdom out of the city's rubbish.

spotlights.name: The Rock Garden

where.label: Sector 1, between the Capitol and Sukhna Lake

spotlights.spot_it: Narrow winding passages and low arches open into courtyards filled with rows of figures, waterfalls of stone and walls set with ceramic and river rocks.
spotlights.story_md: For 18 years almost nobody knew. In **1975** government officials clearing the forest found **12 acres** of courtyards, gorges and thousands of sculptures, built illegally on land where nothing was to be built. They could have bulldozed it. Instead public opinion won, and in **1976** it opened as a public garden, with Nek Chand given a salary and 50 workers. Today it covers about **40 acres**, with more than 5,000 sculptures, waterfalls and a giant swing area, and gets about **3,000 to 4,000 visitors a day**. India Post put it on a stamp in 1983.
spotlights.why_it_matters: In the most rule-bound city in India, the most loved place is one that broke all the rules.
spotlights.memory_hook: Found by accident in 1975, it is now more visited than the Capitol.

spotlights.name: The figure armies
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of identical people, dancers, monkeys, peacocks and soldiers, their bodies coated with broken bangles, crockery or ceramic pieces.
spotlights.story_md: The garden's most famous sight is its **armies**: dozens of figures standing in ranks, as if waiting for a parade. Each body is a frame of recycled iron rods wrapped in cement and then skinned with waste: shards of plates, bits of bathroom tile, glass bangles, slag from furnaces, even the mud-coloured stones from the river beds that Nek Chand called gods. Animals and birds are made the same way. There is also a dolls' museum of about 200 rag dolls made from waste cloth in the 1970s. Up close you can recognise the pattern of someone's teacup.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned the waste of a new city into its most personal art.
spotlights.memory_hook: Armies dressed in broken bangles and teacups.

sections.title: Roses and trees by design
sections.intro_md:
Chandigarh's greenery was planned as carefully as its concrete. The person most responsible was not an architect but an administrator: **M. S. Randhawa**, a botanist, art historian and the city's first chief commissioner, who chose trees for every road, laid out gardens and wrote the classic books on Kangra painting in his spare time.

The result is a city of parks: the Rose Garden, the Leisure Valley's chain of gardens (bougainvillea, terraced, botanical), the green strip through every sector and avenues that flower in turn from spring to monsoon. With few traditional festivals of its own, the city built a calendar around its gardens: the Rose Festival in February, a Mango Festival in summer, and a Carnival in November.

spotlights.name: Zakir Hussain Rose Garden
spotlights.spot_it: Thirty acres of lawns and beds of roses of every colour, fountains, and medicinal trees, crowded with families on February weekends.
spotlights.story_md: The rose garden in Sector 16 was laid out in **1967** under **M. S. Randhawa**, Chandigarh's first chief commissioner, a botanist and art historian who also wrote the standard books on Kangra painting. It covers about **30 acres** with around **50,000 rose bushes of some 1,600 varieties**, and is often called Asia's largest rose garden. It is named after **Zakir Husain**, India's third President. Randhawa also planted medicinal trees like bel, harar and camphor among the beds. Every February it hosts the **Rose Festival**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Randhawa's gardens are why Chandigarh is green, not just geometric.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty thousand roses, planted by a man who also wrote about Kangra painting.

sections.title: How the city lives
sections.intro_md:
Chandigarh is a city of migrants. Its first residents were refugees from West Punjab and government employees from everywhere; today it draws students, doctors, soldiers, IT workers and retirees. Hindi has overtaken Punjabi as the main home language: Punjabi speakers fell from about 36% in 1981 to 22% in 2011. About 81% are Hindu and 13% Sikh.

It is orderly, wealthy and car-loving, with India's highest number of vehicles per person and some of its best schools and hospitals. It also has sharp gaps: rehabilitation colonies and old villages house many of the workers who keep the city running, and the 2011 sex ratio of 818 was among the lowest in India, reflecting both male migration and son preference in the region.

spotlights.name: More cars than people
spotlights.spot_it: Wide, smooth V-roads full of SUVs, roundabouts at every junction, and parked cars filling the green verges of the sectors.
spotlights.story_md: The Seven V's made Chandigarh wonderful to drive and easy to fill with cars. It has the **highest number of vehicles per person in India**: close to **15 lakh registered vehicles** against an estimated **13 lakh people** in 2025. The roundabouts that once kept traffic flowing now jam at rush hour, and parking spills into green belts. The bus system is small, and a metro for the tricity has been approved in principle but is still being studied for cost in 2026. The plan was made for a city of 5 lakh and bicycles.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest case of a plan outgrown by the habits of its people.
spotlights.memory_hook: Built for bicycles, filled with SUVs: more vehicles than residents.

spotlights.name: Sector life
spotlights.spot_it: A row of shops around a parking court in the middle of every sector: chemist, sweet shop, tailor, a dhaba, and a gol market with a roundabout of stalls.
spotlights.story_md: Life in Chandigarh runs at sector scale. Each sector has its market, its school, its park and often its gurdwara, mandir and church. People give directions by sector and house number. The city has a reputation for being clean, polite and quiet: it was ranked India's happiest city in a 2015 survey and in 2025 joined the **Super Swachh League** of the Swachh Survekshan cleanliness survey. It also has some of India's starkest gaps: a sex ratio of just **818 women per 1,000 men** in 2011, and rehabilitation colonies and villages where the poorer third of the city lives.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The sector shapes manners as much as it shapes traffic.
spotlights.memory_hook: Give an address as a house and a sector, and everything is ten minutes away.

sections.title: What the city eats
sections.intro_md:
There is no 'Chandigarh cuisine'. The city eats the food of Punjab, brought in 1947 by refugee families from Lahore, Rawalpindi and the canal colonies, and served in sector-market dhabas, sweet shops and, now, cafes around Sukhna and in the malls.

Breakfast is parathas or chole bhature; lunch is dal, rajma and rice; dinner at a dhaba means butter chicken, dal makhani and tandoori rotis; summer means lassi and mangoes; winter brings sarson da saag with makki di roti from the villages around. The sector market is where food life happens: every sector has its favourite chaat stall, its sweet shop and its late-night tea counter.

spotlights.name: Chole bhature
spotlights.spot_it: A puffed, golden fried bread the size of a plate beside a bowl of dark, spicy chickpeas, with onion rings, pickle and a glass of lassi.
spotlights.story_md: Chandigarh eats the food of the Punjabis who built it: many of the first families were refugees from West Punjab, and they brought the dhabas and sweet shops of Lahore and Rawalpindi. **Chole bhature**, chickpeas cooked dark with tea leaves or amla and spices, eaten with a deep-fried leavened bread, is the city's breakfast of choice, sold from famous stalls in sector markets. With it comes a tall glass of **lassi**. Other favourites are the butter chicken and dal makhani of the old dhabas, and kulche with chhole.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Its food is a living map of where its first residents came from.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bread the size of a plate, chickpeas as dark as tea.

sections.title: A factory of champions
sections.intro_md:
For a small city, Chandigarh has produced or nurtured a startling list of sportspeople: a World Cup-winning captain, the Flying Sikh, the first Indian on the European golf tour, a batsman who hit six sixes in an over, and India's first individual Olympic gold medallist. Its good schools, Army and Air Force stations nearby, a cricket stadium in Sector 16 and the Punjab Cricket Association stadium in Mohali help explain it. So does Partition: several of these families came as refugees, with a hunger to start again.

Shooting, golf, hockey and cricket are the city's strengths, and the tricity's academies keep feeding national teams.

spotlights.name: Kapil Dev
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, smiling fast bowler with a wide open-chested action, and in 1983 lifting the World Cup on the Lord's balcony.
spotlights.story_md: Kapil Dev was born in Chandigarh in 1959 to a family that had come from Montgomery (now Sahiwal) in West Punjab after Partition. He learnt the game in the city before becoming the greatest all-rounder India has produced. In 1983, aged 24, he captained India to its first **World Cup**, still the youngest winning captain. In that tournament he scored **175 not out against Zimbabwe** after India were 17 for 5, an innings that was never filmed because of a BBC strike. He retired with **434 Test wickets**, then a world record, and was named Wisden's Indian Cricketer of the Century in 2002.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He changed Indian cricket from a game of spinners and batsmen to one that could win.
spotlights.memory_hook: 175 not out, and no camera rolling.

spotlights.name: Milkha Singh
spotlights.spot_it: A lean runner with a long beard tied under his chin and a patka, flying around the bend of a cinder track.
spotlights.story_md: Milkha Singh was a child of the Partition: his parents and siblings were killed in the violence in 1947, and he crossed to India as an orphan. In the Army he became a runner. In **1958** he won the **Commonwealth Games** 440 yards gold in Cardiff, independent India's first. At the **Rome Olympics of 1960** he finished fourth in the 400 m in 45.73 seconds, a national record for almost 40 years. Pakistan's President Ayub Khan named him the 'Flying Sikh' after he beat Abdul Khaliq in Lahore in 1960. He lived in Chandigarh for decades and died there on 18 June 2021, aged 91.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the city's most beloved resident and the face of what Partition cost and what it made.
spotlights.memory_hook: Orphaned by Partition, named by Pakistan's president, at home in Sector 8.

spotlights.name: Yuvraj Singh
spotlights.spot_it: A tall left-handed batsman with a high backlift, launching the ball over the leg side.
spotlights.story_md: Yuvraj Singh was born in Chandigarh in 1981, the son of a former Test cricketer. On **19 September 2007** at Durban, in the first T20 World Cup, he hit England's Stuart Broad for **six sixes in an over** and reached 50 in 12 balls, still a record in T20 internationals. In **2011** he was Player of the Tournament as India won the World Cup at home, while he was ill with what was later diagnosed as a rare cancer between his lungs. He came back to international cricket after chemotherapy and later set up a cancer charity.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the purest example of the sports factory that the tricity became.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six balls, six sixes, Durban 2007.

spotlights.name: Abhinav Bindra
spotlights.spot_it: A shooter in a stiff canvas jacket, one eye closed, holding an air rifle dead still for a 10 m target.
spotlights.story_md: On **11 August 2008** in Beijing, Abhinav Bindra won the **10 m air rifle** with a last shot of 10.8, becoming **India's first individual Olympic gold medallist**. Born in Dehradun in 1982 to a Punjabi family, he went to St. Stephen's School in Chandigarh and made the tricity his base. In the final he was the only shooter who never scored below 10.0, and he was level with Finland's Henri Häkkinen before the last shot. Since retiring in 2016 he has joined the IOC Athletes' Commission (2018) and runs a foundation that brings sports science to Indian athletes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India waited 108 years for an individual Olympic gold, and it came from a Chandigarh schoolboy.
spotlights.memory_hook: One shot of 10.8 for India's first individual gold.

sections.title: Whose city is it?
sections.intro_md:
In 1966 Punjab was split on language lines, and both the new Punjab and the new Haryana wanted Chandigarh. The Centre made it a Union Territory 'for now'. Sixty years later 'for now' still holds. Punjab argues it was built as Punjab's capital, on Punjab's land, to replace Lahore. Haryana argues it has an equal share and will not give it up without territory in return.

The dispute has cost lives, inspired fasts unto death and appeared in a national peace accord with a fixed date that passed. It still flares: in 2025 a bill to change the city's constitutional status united every party in Punjab against it within days.

spotlights.name: Two states, one capital
spotlights.spot_it: Look at the Capitol: one Assembly building, one Secretariat, one High Court, each shared by Punjab and Haryana.
spotlights.story_md: On **1 November 1966** the Punjab Reorganisation Act split Punjab on linguistic lines: Hindi-speaking Haryana was carved out, hill districts went to Himachal Pradesh, and the Punjabi-speaking remainder kept the name. Both new states claimed Chandigarh. As a stopgap, the city became a **Union Territory** run by the Centre and the **joint capital** of both states. It was meant to be temporary. Almost 60 years later, two governments and two legislatures still work from Le Corbusier's buildings, and since 1984 the Governor of Punjab has also been the UT's Administrator.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the oldest unsettled disputes between Indian states.
spotlights.memory_hook: One capital, two states, sixty years of 'temporary'.

spotlights.name: Darshan Singh Pheruman
spotlights.spot_it: An elderly Sikh leader and former freedom fighter who fasted in prison until he died, for Chandigarh to go to Punjab.
spotlights.story_md: After 1966 the Akali Dal demanded Chandigarh for Punjab. Sant Fateh Singh began a fast and threatened to burn himself in December 1966, then ended it on a promise of arbitration. Darshan Singh Pheruman, an old Congress and Akali freedom fighter, accused him of breaking his vow and in August 1969 began a **fast unto death** in jail. He refused all food and died on **27 October 1969**, on the 74th day. Within months, in January 1970, Indira Gandhi announced that Chandigarh would go to Punjab in five years, with Haryana getting money for a new capital. It never happened.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His death shows how deeply Punjab feels about the city.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 74-day fast for a city that stayed in limbo.

spotlights.name: The Rajiv-Longowal Accord
spotlights.spot_it: A typed, signed agreement between a young Prime Minister and a Sikh leader, whose Chandigarh clause had a fixed date: 26 January 1986.
spotlights.story_md: After Operation Blue Star and the assassination of Indira Gandhi, Rajiv Gandhi signed an accord with the Akali leader **Harchand Singh Longowal** on **24 July 1985** to end the Punjab crisis. One clause said Chandigarh would be transferred to Punjab on **26 January 1986**, with Hindi-speaking areas of Punjab going to Haryana in exchange. Less than a month later, on 20 August 1985, Longowal was shot dead by militants. The two states could not agree on which villages to swap, and the date passed. The clause has never been carried out.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the closest Chandigarh has come to belonging to one state.
spotlights.memory_hook: A transfer with a date, and the date passed.

spotlights.name: The Article 240 row
spotlights.spot_it: Headlines in Punjab papers about a 'Chandigarh bill', and protests by every major Punjab party at once.
spotlights.story_md: In November 2025 a parliamentary bulletin listed the **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2025**, which would bring Chandigarh under **Article 240**. That article lets the President make regulations directly for certain Union Territories without legislatures, which critics read as a step towards a separate Lieutenant Governor and away from Punjab's claim. AAP, Congress and the Akali Dal all condemned it as anti-Punjab, and Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann said it would not be allowed. The Home Ministry said no final decision had been taken and that it would not bring the bill in the winter session.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The dispute is not history; it can still unite Punjab's rival parties overnight.
spotlights.memory_hook: A one-line bill that united Punjab's quarrelling parties in a week.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
A city with a famous designer collects myths. The commonest is that **Le Corbusier designed Chandigarh**: he made the master plan and the Capitol, but most of the city was designed by Jeanneret, Drew, Fry and Indian architects. Another is that the city was **built on empty land**: it displaced dozens of villages and sits on Harappan remains. A third is that it is **perfectly planned**: about a third of residents live in villages, colonies and settlements the plan never imagined.

Some odd stories are true. There really is **no Sector 13** in the original plan. The Open Hand really does **turn in the wind**. Chandigarh really does have **more vehicles than people**. And the Rock Garden really was **illegal** for 18 years.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
The last three years have kept Chandigarh in the national news. In February 2024 the Supreme Court overturned its mayoral election. In February 2025 a wall of the Rock Garden came down for High Court parking, and residents hugged trees in protest. In July 2025 it joined the Super Swachh League of India's cleanest cities. In November 2025 a bill to place it under Article 240 caused uproar in Punjab and was put on hold.

In 2026 the BJP won the mayor's post in January by an open show of hands; a long-promised tricity metro, approved in principle, was still stuck on cost; in June a Paris auction of stolen Jeanneret chairs was halted for the first time; and on 15 October Sukhna Lake became India's 103rd Ramsar wetland.

spotlights.name: The mayor's election and the eight ballots
spotlights.spot_it: Video footage of a returning officer marking ballot papers with a pen, shown in the Supreme Court.
spotlights.story_md: On **30 January 2024** the returning officer at Chandigarh's mayoral election, **Anil Masih**, declared eight votes for the AAP-Congress candidate invalid and announced the BJP's candidate as mayor. CCTV footage showed him marking the ballots. The Supreme Court, under Chief Justice D. Y. Chandrachud, examined the ballot papers itself and on **20 February 2024** declared AAP's **Kuldeep Kumar** mayor, holding that Masih had deliberately defaced the votes, and ordered proceedings against him. It was the first time the court had itself counted votes to name the winner of a municipal poll. In January 2026 the BJP's Saurabh Joshi won the post in an open show of hands.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small city election became a national lesson in vote counting.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eight ballot papers, one pen, one Supreme Court recount.

spotlights.name: Sukhna becomes a Ramsar site
spotlights.spot_it: The same lake promenade, now with an international wetland label.
spotlights.story_md: On **15 October 2026** the Union environment minister announced that **Sukhna Lake** had been added to the Ramsar list of wetlands of international importance, with Sauj Jheel in Uttar Pradesh, taking India's count to **103**. The listing names its role as a wintering stop on the Central Asian Flyway for threatened species such as the common pochard and Pallas's fish eagle. It also brings duties: the lake has lost more than half its water-holding capacity to silt, and Ramsar status puts pressure on the administration to stop building in its catchment and keep it from drying out.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A planner's reservoir is now officially a wetland of world importance.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's 103rd Ramsar site was built by engineers in 1958.

spotlights.name: The Rock Garden wall comes down
spotlights.spot_it: Bulldozers at the outer wall of the Rock Garden, and citizens hugging trees nearby in a small Chipko-style protest.
spotlights.story_md: In **February 2025** the administration demolished a stretch of the Rock Garden's outer wall and began cutting trees to widen a road and make parking for the High Court next door. Residents' groups protested with placards reading 'Sorry Nek Chand', hugged trees in a nod to the Chipko movement, and argued that the clearance covered only a small stretch of road widening, not a car park. The administration said the work was needed to ease traffic. The episode summed up the city's dilemma: a heritage plan and an artist's garden versus the cars and courts of a growing region.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Heritage is not settled once it is famous; it has to be defended project by project.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sorry Nek Chand: a wall of his garden lost to parking.

sections.title: Recap: the city in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. Chandigarh was built because Partition gave Punjab's capital, Lahore, to Pakistan.
2. It is named after the goddess Chandi, whose temple stands nearby.
3. Albert Mayer and Matthew Nowicki planned it first; Nowicki's death in 1950 brought in Le Corbusier.
4. The city is a grid of sectors of about 800 by 1,200 m, with seven ranks of roads and no Sector 13.
5. The Capitol Complex, a World Heritage Site since 2016, has the High Court, Assembly, Secretariat and the turning Open Hand.
6. Pierre Jeanneret built much of the rest, and his furniture became a global collector's item, often stolen.
7. Nek Chand built the Rock Garden in secret from waste; it opened in 1976.
8. Since 1966 it has been a Union Territory and the shared capital of Punjab and Haryana, still disputed.
9. Kapil Dev, Milkha Singh, Yuvraj Singh and Abhinav Bindra all belong to its story.
10. It has more vehicles than people, and in 2026 its lake became a Ramsar wetland.

side_dish.title: How to design a shadow
side_dish.body_md:
Le Corbusier's Tower of Shadows is a physics lesson you can walk into. The sun's path across the sky changes with the season and with your latitude. Chandigarh is at about 30.7° north. At noon on the June solstice the sun is almost overhead, about 83° above the southern horizon; at noon in late December it is only about 36° up. In the morning and evening it is low in the east and west all year.

That gives three simple rules. On a **south** wall, a horizontal overhang works: it blocks the high summer sun and lets the low winter sun in. On **east and west** walls, the sun is low, so horizontal shades fail; you need **vertical fins**, or a deep grid of both, which is what the Secretariat's **brise-soleil** is. A **north** wall in India barely needs shading at all.

Le Corbusier drew sun-path diagrams for each facade, then sized the concrete fins and ledges so that the hot sun would not touch the glass in summer. The High Court goes further: its parasol roof shades the whole building and leaves a gap for wind to carry heat away.

You can test it at home. Note when sunlight first and last falls on your window in a day, and how far into the room it reaches at noon. In summer and winter you will get very different answers. That difference is what a good shade is designed around.

offline_task.title: Read your own neighbourhood like a sector
offline_task.body_md:
Walk for 20 minutes around where you live and look at it the way Chandigarh's planners would.

1. Draw a rough rectangle of the area you can reach on foot in ten minutes. Mark the places you actually go: shop, chemist, school, park, place of worship, bus stop.
2. Classify every road you cross into Le Corbusier's ranks: a road that links cities (V1), a big avenue (V2), a fast road with no doors on it (V3), a shopping street (V4), a local loop (V5), a lane to houses (V6), a footpath or park path (V7).
3. Note where the plan fails: places you cannot walk to, roads with no footpath, a market with no shade.
4. Look for one object designed with care, like a bench, a drain cover, a railing or a door, and one that clearly was not.

Write three lines: what your neighbourhood does better than a Chandigarh sector, what it does worse, and one change you would make.

best_facts.fact: Nek Chand, a government road inspector, secretly built a garden of thousands of sculptures from the city's waste for about 18 years before officials stumbled on it in 1975.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most rule-bound city in India's favourite place was illegal.

best_facts.fact: Chandigarh looks like Le Corbusier's city partly because its first architect, Matthew Nowicki, died in a plane crash in Egypt in 1950.
best_facts.why_surprising: A city's look was decided by an air accident.

best_facts.fact: The 50-tonne metal hand of the Open Hand monument turns in the wind on ball bearings. It was built in 1985, 20 years after Le Corbusier died.
best_facts.why_surprising: A monument that is also a weathervane, finished by others.

best_facts.fact: Pierre Jeanneret's office chairs were once sold off as government scrap; more than 100 sales abroad since 2009 have fetched an estimated ₹40 to 50 crore, and in June 2026 a Paris auction was halted for the first time.
best_facts.why_surprising: Junk became design treasure, then evidence in an FIR.

best_facts.fact: The planned city of the future is named after a village goddess: Chandigarh means 'fort of Chandi'.
Chandigarh has no Sector 13 in its original plan.
Chandigarh has more registered vehicles than people: close to 15 lakh vehicles against about 13 lakh residents in 2025.
best_facts.why_surprising: A city drawn for bicycles has the most cars per head in India.

best_facts.fact: About 40% of the Lahore Museum's collection came to India in 1948, and it is in Chandigarh's Government Museum.
Kapil Dev's 175 not out against Zimbabwe in 1983, one of the great one-day innings, was never filmed because of a BBC strike.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most famous innings by a Chandigarh boy exists only in memory.

best_facts.fact: In February 2024 the Supreme Court examined ballot papers itself and declared the winner of Chandigarh's mayoral election, after finding the returning officer had defaced eight votes.
best_facts.why_surprising: The country's highest court counted a municipal vote.

best_facts.fact: Pierre Jeanneret, who built much of the city, asked for his ashes to be scattered in Sukhna Lake; they were, in 1970.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Swiss architect chose a Punjab reservoir as his grave.

best_facts.fact: Chandigarh's manhole covers carry a relief map of the city's master plan.
best_facts.why_surprising: The city prints its map on its drains.

best_facts.fact: Darshan Singh Pheruman fasted for 74 days in 1969 to get Chandigarh for Punjab and died; nearly 60 years on, the city still belongs to neither state.
best_facts.why_surprising: A life given for a question still unanswered.

best_facts.fact: The Rajiv-Longowal Accord fixed 26 January 1986 as the day Chandigarh would go to Punjab. The day passed and nothing happened.
best_facts.why_surprising: A dated promise in a national accord, never kept.

best_facts.fact: Sukhna Lake, a reservoir made by damming a seasonal stream in 1958, became India's 103rd Ramsar wetland in October 2026.
best_facts.why_surprising: An engineers' lake is now a wetland of world importance.

best_facts.fact: Chandigarh's sex ratio in 2011 was 818 women for every 1,000 men, one of the lowest in India.
best_facts.why_surprising: The 'City Beautiful' has a stark gender gap.

best_facts.fact: The Assembly chamber's roof is shaped like a power-station cooling tower.
